title: Surgery
tagline: The surgical patient, anaesthesia, trauma, the acute abdomen and the main surgical specialties
summary: Surgery treats disease by operation, and every doctor looks after surgical patients. This course covers perioperative care, anaesthesia and pain relief, wounds and surgical infection, trauma, the acute abdomen, and gastrointestinal, breast and endocrine, vascular and urological, and orthopaedic surgery.
overview: An operation is a controlled injury: the surgeon damages tissue so that the patient ends up better off. Whether that trade succeeds depends as much on what happens before and after the operation as on the operation itself. This course teaches the principles that apply to every surgical patient and then the common emergency and elective conditions that a junior doctor on a surgical team meets.

The first four chapters cover the general principles: preoperative assessment and optimisation, fluids, and postoperative complications in the order in which they appear; general and regional anaesthesia, airway management, anaesthetic emergencies and acute pain; wound healing, surgical-site infection and necrotising soft-tissue infection; and the assessment and resuscitation of injured patients, including head injury and burns. The remaining chapters cover the acute abdomen; hernias, gallstones, gastrointestinal cancers, inflammatory bowel disease, stomas and bariatric surgery; breast, thyroid, parathyroid and adrenal surgery; arterial and venous disease and the main urological conditions; and fractures, orthopaedic emergencies, bone and joint infection and joint replacement.

Throughout, the emphasis is on decisions: which patient needs an operation now, which needs resuscitation first, which needs imaging, and how to explain the situation clearly to a senior colleague and to the patient. Each chapter includes worked clinical cases and calculations. Guidance is UK-first (NICE and the relevant specialist bodies) and dated; all cases are fictional, and management is described as principle rather than as instructions for individual patients.
outcomes: Explain the surgical stress response and assess fitness for surgery, including risk scoring, optimisation, medicine management, fasting and consent based on material risks.
Prescribe maintenance intravenous fluids in principle and recognise postoperative complications by their typical timing, including anastomotic leak, venous thromboembolism and delirium.
Describe general and regional anaesthesia, airway management and minimum monitoring, and recognise and outline the management of anaphylaxis, malignant hyperthermia and local anaesthetic toxicity.
Plan multimodal analgesia that limits opioid harm, and calculate local anaesthetic dose limits and PONV risk.
Explain wound healing and its failures, and outline the prevention, recognition and treatment of surgical-site infection, abscesses, necrotising soft-tissue infection and wound dehiscence.
Apply the primary survey and damage control resuscitation to an injured patient, and recognise life-threatening chest, abdominal, pelvic, head and burn injuries.
Assess a patient with acute abdominal pain, distinguish inflammation, obstruction, perforation and ischaemia, and know when emergency surgery is needed.
Outline the investigation and surgical management of hernias, gallstones, gastrointestinal cancers, inflammatory bowel disease, anorectal disease, stomas and obesity.
Describe triple assessment and the surgical management of breast cancer, and the assessment and surgery of thyroid nodules, hyperparathyroidism and adrenal tumours.

Recognise limb ischaemia, aortic aneurysm, testicular torsion, the obstructed infected kidney and other vascular and urological emergencies, and apply fracture principles, the hip fracture pathway and the management of orthopaedic emergencies.

history.title: Public demonstration of anaesthesia
history.detail: On 16 October 1846 William Morton gave ether to a patient at the Massachusetts General Hospital while John Collins Warren removed a tumour from his neck. Crawford Long had used ether in 1842 without publishing, and Horace Wells's demonstration of nitrous oxide in 1845 had been judged a failure. Within a year anaesthesia was in use worldwide.

history.title: Handwashing and puerperal fever
history.detail: Ignaz Semmelweis showed in Vienna that puerperal fever was far commoner on the ward staffed by doctors coming from the autopsy room, and that washing hands in chlorinated lime solution greatly reduced deaths. His work was largely rejected in his lifetime.

history.title: Antiseptic surgery
history.detail: Joseph Lister, applying Louis Pasteur's germ theory, treated compound fractures and wounds with carbolic acid in Glasgow and reported falling rates of infection and amputation in The Lancet. Antisepsis gave way to asepsis, with steam sterilisation and, from about 1890, rubber gloves introduced by William Halsted.

history.title: Safe thyroid surgery
history.detail: Theodor Kocher in Bern reduced the mortality of thyroidectomy to well under 1% through meticulous technique, and his observation of hypothyroidism after total thyroidectomy helped reveal the function of the gland. He received the Nobel Prize in 1909.

history.title: X-rays
history.detail: Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays, which were used to image fractures and foreign bodies within weeks and transformed the diagnosis of injury.

history.title: Low-friction hip replacement
history.detail: At Wrightington Hospital, John Charnley developed the low-friction total hip replacement, with a small metal head on high-density polyethylene fixed with acrylic cement, and introduced clean-air theatre enclosures to reduce infection.

history.title: Advanced Trauma Life Support
history.detail: After the disorganised care his family received following a plane crash in rural Nebraska in 1976, the orthopaedic surgeon James Styner and colleagues ran the first Advanced Trauma Life Support course; the American College of Surgeons adopted it in 1980, and it is now taught worldwide.

history.title: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy
history.detail: Erich Mühe in Germany performed the first laparoscopic cholecystectomy in 1985; from 1987 Philippe Mouret in Lyon and François Dubois in Paris popularised the technique, which began the era of minimally invasive general surgery.

history.title: The surgical safety checklist
history.detail: Alex Haynes, Atul Gawande and colleagues reported that introducing the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist in eight hospitals in eight countries was followed by a fall in inpatient deaths from 1.5% to 0.8% and in major complications from 11.0% to 7.0%. The checklist is now used routinely in most countries.
